function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete “what‑to‑do” guide** that you can copy into your local clone of `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and a GitHub Actions workflow that match a typical Node.js web app (the repo’s README shows it listens on port 3000).  

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here, but the instructions below will get you through the whole process on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json + lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> * • Uses a small Alpine base → smaller image.*  
> * • Copies `package*.json` first → Docker cache works well for dependency installs.*  
> * • Installs only production deps → keeps the image lean.*  
> * • Exposes port 3000 (the app’s listening port).*  

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or split into two files if you prefer) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you don’t have an LB
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port
    targetPort: 3000          # Container port
```

> *What to change:*  
> * Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).  
> * If you’re running locally without a cloud LB, switch `type` to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.*

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ${{ secrets.REGISTRY }}/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} .

    - name: Log in to registry & push image
      env:
        REGISTRY: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY }}
        REGISTRY_USER: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }}
        REGISTRY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }}
      run: |
        echo "$REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | docker login $REGISTRY -u $REGISTRY_USER --password-stdin
        docker push $REGISTRY/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `REGISTRY` – e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq`  
> * `REGISTRY_USER` – your registry username (often your GitHub username for GHCR)  
> * `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` – your registry password/token (GHCR token with `write:packages` scope)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the next push to `main`, building the Docker image, running tests, and pushing the image to your registry.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow finishes, you should see a new image in your registry tagged with the commit SHA. You can deploy it to a cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

…and verify the pod is running:

```bash
kubectl get pods
kubectl logs <pod-name>
```

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., missing secrets, registry auth errors), let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
